slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 24: Appendix C — Generic Arithmetic and Range-Lifetime Labs. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 24, treat Requirement and simplest approach as a design decision with costs and evidence. Sum a read-only sequence of integer values. Empty input produces zero. Every intermediate addition must be representable in the selected type, or the operation rejects it without modifying caller-owned input. Boolean and floating-point arguments are outside this particular API’s domain. A generic signature must communicate those restrictions without pretending that a concept proves the arithmetic safe. The unsafe shortcut adds first and checks the result afterward. For signed overflow, that can already have left the language’s defined behavior. The reference compares against safe thresholds before addition. For unsigned values, it checks whether the right operand exceeds the remaining room below the maximum. For signed values, it handles positive and negative right operands separately so the threshold expressions remain representable. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: Evidence and interpretation
keyPoints: The concept expresses a compile-time category: integral types except Boolean.
The runtime checks express value-dependent representability.
These responsibilities are different.
An integer type can satisfy the concept while two values of that type cannot be added safely.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 24, treat Evidence and interpretation as a design decision with costs and evidence. The concept expresses a compile-time category: integral types except Boolean. The runtime checks express value-dependent representability. These responsibilities are different. An integer type can satisfy the concept while two values of that type cannot be added safely. Conversely, a floating-point value that happens to be exactly integral remains outside the declared type domain. The boundary cases include maximum plus zero, minimum plus zero, one step inward from each bound, and one step beyond each bound. A multi-element total fails late enough to demonstrate that earlier local progress does not mutate the caller’s vector. The total is held in local state and returned only after all additions succeed. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 24, treat Requirement and model as a design decision with costs and evidence. A function with local input must return an owning selected result. A temporary span over an external array may expose a valid iterator while the array remains alive. A temporary owning vector passed to a ranges search must not yield an ordinary retained iterator through that algorithm’s safe return type. A view used before a source change should not be reused under an assumption that cached membership state automatically resets. The experiment demonstrates these distinctions through valid executions and static assertions. It does not create a dangling view and dereference it merely to obtain a sanitizer screenshot. A type-level check or a correctly scoped ownership trace is often a better teaching experiment than deliberately invoking undefined behavior. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: Evidence and interpretation
keyPoints: selected_snapshot constructs a local input vector and a lazy pipeline, then materializes the selected squares into.
Returning that vector does not retain a borrow of the local source.
Its values are checked after the function returns, when the source no longer exists.
The result’s independence comes from ownership, not from the fact that the pipeline used modern syntax.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 24, treat Evidence and interpretation as a design decision with costs and evidence. selected_snapshot constructs a local input vector and a lazy pipeline, then materializes the selected squares into an owning vector. Returning that vector does not retain a borrow of the local source. Its values are checked after the function returns, when the source no longer exists. The result’s independence comes from ownership, not from the fact that the pipeline used modern syntax. The borrowed-range assertions distinguish the span wrapper from an owning vector. The temporary span’s data belongs to a still-live local array in the caller. That valid array lifetime is essential; borrowed-range status would not rescue a span pointing into destroyed storage. The temporary-vector search instead has a dangling result type, making the unsafe retained-iterator use unavailable through that result. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 24, treat Guided extension as a design decision with costs and evidence. Design two APIs for selecting task titles. One returns an owning vector of strings. The other returns a view intended for immediate use over a caller-owned immutable collection. Write their lifetime contracts side by side. Test the owning result after the input is replaced; consume the borrowed result only within its valid scope. Explain which interface is suitable for queuing work to a later stage and why. Technical references: concepts, constraints, ranges, filter views, and object lifetime.
